The user wants a 2-3 sentence news wire style summary of this article. Key points:

1. The Taliban published a biography of Mullah Mohammed Omar, apparently to dispel rumors that he is dead and to reaffirm he is still their leader.
2. The reclusive founder hasn't been seen or heard from since 2001; US offers $10 million reward.
3. The biography also appears to be a response to ISIS's al-Baghdadi declaring himself caliph, asserting Omar's jihadi leadership credentials.

Terse wire style: "The Taliban has published a biography of founder Mullah Mohammed Omar in an apparent bid to dispel rumors he is dead and reaffirm his leadership. The reclusive one-eyed leader has not been seen or heard from since the 2001 US-led invasion toppled the Taliban. The document also appears timed to counter ISIS leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi's declaration of a caliphate, analysts say."

That's 3 sentences, terse. Output only the summaryThe Taliban has published a biography of founder Mullah Mohammed Omar in an apparent bid to dispel rumors of his death and reaffirm his leadership. The reclusive one-eyed leader, who carries a $10 million US bounty, has not been seen or heard from since the 2001 US-led invasion toppled the Taliban. Analysts say the document also appears aimed at countering ISIS leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi's declaration of a caliphate.

Hundreds gathered in South Carolina for the funeral of Walter Scott, where mourners and family called his death a catalyst for change. Officer Michael Slager faces murder charges after cellphone video captured him shooting the fleeing Scott in the back. New details reveal Scott ran due to outstanding child support debt, while the officer's defense team suggests a manslaughter charge is more appropriate.

A former TSA agent was sentenced to six months in jail for secretly recording a female co-worker in a bathroom and burglarizing her home. Daniel Boykin, 33, pleaded guilty to unlawful photography and aggravated burglary after police found over 1,500 photos and 90 videos of the victim on his devices. He received an additional five and a half years of probation and has been terminated from the agency.

Lacking natural resources, Cape Verde is leveraging its rich musical heritage to diversify and boost its economy. The government and private sector are promoting events like the Atlantic Music Expo and Kriol Jazz Festival to gain international exposure and drive tourism. Officials hope this focus on the creative industries will establish a sustainable economic model for the island nation.

Aaron defeated Burnley 1-0 to move within four points of Premier League leaders Chelsea. Aston Villa and Leicester City secured vital wins in the relegation battle, while Crystal Palace routed Sunderland 4-1.

The original cast of Twin Peaks launched a #SaveTwinPeaks campaign supporting David Lynch's exit from Showtime over a salary dispute. The stars argue that filming the revival without the co-creator is akin to "pies without cherries." Showtime maintains hope for a resolution, though Lynch states the offered budget was insufficient.
Andrew Getty, heir to the Getty oil fortune, died at 47. Police reported no foul play, citing a preliminary assessment of natural causes and a history of health issues. An autopsy is pending.

The user wants a 2-3 sentence news wire style summary of this article. Key facts:

- Nyia Parler, 41, mother of a quadriplegic 21-year-old man with cerebral palsy
- Left her son in Cobbs Creek Park woods in Philadelphia on April 6 while she went to Maryland to visit her boyfriend
- He was found Friday after more than four days, suffering dehydration, malnutrition, eye problems, cut to back
- She was taken into custody in Maryland but cannot be extradited until she completes unspecified "treatment"
- She faces charges of aggravated assault, simple assault, recklessly endangering another person

Terse news wire style. 2-3 short sentences. OutputA Maryland woman accused of abandoning her quadriplegic son in a Philadelphia park for more than four days cannot be extradited until she completes unspecified treatment, police said. Nyia Parler, 41, left the 21-year-old, who also has cerebral palsy, in Cobbs Creek Park while traveling to visit her boyfriend in Maryland, according to authorities. She faces charges including aggravated assault and recklessly endangering another person.

NASA astrophysicist Amy Mainzer has named an asteroid after Nobel laureate and education activist Malala Yousafzai. The celestial body, designated 316201 Malala, orbits the sun between Mars and Jupiter every five and a half years. Mainzer said she chose the name to honor women's contributions and highlight the need for girls' education worldwide.

A gastrointestinal illness has sickened 100 passengers and crew aboard the cruise ship Celebrity Infinity. The CDC is investigating the cause of the outbreak and will meet the vessel in San Diego on Monday. Celebrity Cruises has increased cleaning and disinfection procedures in response.

The "Star Wars" saga was released on digital HD, while actress Mindy Kaling's brother revealed he faked being black to get into medical school. Burger King offered to pay for a couple's wedding due to their combined surname, and fans mourned the death of "Dukes of Hazzard" actor James Best.

The FBI charged a Philadelphia woman for attempting to travel overseas to join ISIS. Two New York women were also arrested this week on separate terror charges for plotting domestic attacks. Officials warn the decentralized terrorist threat increasingly relies on social media and lone wolf actors.
HBO released a teaser for the second season of "True Detective," premiering June 21. Colin Farrell, Vince Vaughn, Rachel McAdams, and Taylor Kitsch star in the new California-set crime drama.

Massachusetts authorities charged Carlos Colina, 32, with assault and improper disposal of a body after human remains were found in a Cambridge duffel bag and apartment building. The victim was identified as 26-year-old Jonathan Camilien, who was acquainted with Colina. Officials say additional charges may be pending as the investigation continues.

Louisville basketball star Trey Moses invited freshman Ellie Meredith, who has Down syndrome, to prom. The gesture, captured in a viral photo, drew praise for the student athlete. Moses, a Ball State recruit, said he wanted to ensure Ellie felt included.

NBC debuts the 12-week miniseries "A.D. The Bible Continues" on Sunday, alongside the final episodes of AMC's "Mad Men." The week's additional premieres include NBC's "American Odyssey," FX's "Louie" and "The Comedians," and Netflix's "Marvel's Daredevil."

Indiana Governor Mike Pence signed a controversial religious freedom law to bolster his conservative credentials for a potential 2016 White House bid. The resulting backlash is dragging the Republican field to the right, forcing candidates to address "religious freedom" legislation. Despite national progress on LGBT rights, the issue looks set to dominate the upcoming election cycle.

Apple released a mobile OS update introducing diverse emoji options, including varied skin tones and same-sex couple emojis. The expanded representation drew both praise and criticism, with some groups noting notable absences like redheads and the Armenian flag.

Singer Avril Lavigne revealed she was bedridden for five months suffering from Lyme disease. The star told People magazine she felt like she was dying during the ordeal, but is now recovering and preparing to release new music.

The user wants a 2-3 sentence news wire style summary of this article about Anne Frank's death date being revised by new research.

Key points:
- New research from the Anne Frank House shows Anne and her sister Margot died at least a month earlier than previously thought
- Previously believed she died March 31, 1945, just two weeks before Bergen-Belsen was liberated
- Researchers re-examined Red Cross archives, ITS, Bergen-Belsen Memorial, and survivor testimonies
- Both sisters likely died of typhus in February 1945
- Exact dates remain unclear

News wire style is terse, factual, leads with the news. Let me draft:

"New research by the Anne Frank House suggests Anne Frank and her sister Margot died at least a month earlier than previously believed, likely in February 1945 rather than March. The findings, based on Red Cross archives and survivor testimonies, indicate the sisters died of typhus at Bergen-Belsen before the camp's liberation. Exact dates of death remain unknown."

That's three sentences, terse, factual. Good.New research by the Anne Frank House indicates Anne Frank and her sister Margot died at least a month earlier than previously believed, likely in February 1945 rather than late March. The findings, based on Red Cross archives and survivor testimonies, suggest both sisters died of typhus at Bergen-Belsen before the camp's liberation. Exact dates of death remain unknown.

Two Troy University students were arrested and charged with sexual battery after police discovered video evidence of an alleged gang rape in Panama City Beach. The suspects have been suspended from the university, and authorities anticipate further arrests.

A stray dog in Washington State survived being hit by a car, struck with a hammer, and buried in a field. The dog, named Theia, requires extensive surgery for severe injuries, prompting a fundraising campaign that has exceeded its goal. Her foster owner describes the one-year-old bully breed mix as a "miracle dog" who is gentle and loving despite her ordeal.

The FBI confirmed Malaysian bomb maker Zulkifli bin Hir, known as Marwan, was killed in a botched Philippine raid in January. The operation left 44 police commandos dead and shattered a three-year ceasefire with rebel forces, threatening a fragile peace agreement.

A lawmaker criticized the recent Iran nuclear framework, arguing President Obama conceded too much leverage by easing sanctions. The author warned the deal allows Iran to keep its nuclear infrastructure, funds terrorism, and lacks sufficient inspection safeguards to prevent a secret weapons program.

AMC's "Mad Men" returns for its final season, navigating the disintegration of the 1960s and the advertising world amid historical events like the Manson murders and Woodstock. Creator Matthew Weiner remains tight-lipped about the finale, though the series is expected to explore the agency's struggle for survival following its McCann Erickson acquisition. The conclusion may find protagonist Don Draper facing a ban on cigarette advertising, leaving him alone and inscrutable as the era ends.

A Dallas Zoo giraffe named Katie gave birth to a six-foot calf Friday evening in an hour-long labor streamed live by Animal Planet. The newborn, following a 15-month gestation, showed positive signs including moving its ears and attempting to nurse.

Loretta Lynch's confirmation wait for attorney general has dragged on longer than the previous eight nominees combined, sparking accusations of racial bias. While Republicans attribute the delay to partisan legislative battles, Democrats and supporters argue she is being unfairly obstructed. If confirmed, Lynch would become the first African-American woman to hold the post.

Three people were killed and five wounded when armed assailants stormed the attorney general's office in northern Afghanistan. Afghan security forces remain engaged in an ongoing firefight with the attackers as they cautiously work to secure the building.

Bob Barker, 91, returned to host "The Price Is Right" for the first time since his 2007 retirement. The television legend led the show's first game on the April 1 broadcast before handing duties back to current host Drew Carey.
Blues legend B.B. King was hospitalized for dehydration caused by Type II diabetes. The 89-year-old guitarist has returned home to rest after stating he felt "much better."

Dzhokhar Tsarnaev was found guilty on all counts for the Boston Marathon bombing. The author argues that preventing future radicalization requires addressing Muslim grievances rather than reforming Islam. Extremism is ultimately defeated by showing young Muslims that violence harms their community.

CNN rounds up the week's top videos, featuring a tour of Mike Tyson's abandoned Ohio mansion and a ride on the world's fastest giga-coaster. Additional clips include an exclusive interview with the creator of Bikram yoga regarding sexual assault allegations and a witness account of the Germanwings crash.

A Pentagon map indicates coalition forces have reclaimed 25-30% of ISIS-held territory in Iraq. Analysts note that while these frontal gains damage ISIS prestige, the group compensates for losses through asymmetric attacks elsewhere. The strategy lacks maneuverist warfare capabilities needed to rapidly disrupt ISIS command and control.

An Air Canada passenger attempted to strangle a sleeping passenger with a headphone cord during a descent into Atlanta. The suspect was removed by authorities and transported for a medical evaluation, while the victim was unhurt. The FBI stated no federal charges are currently pending.

A British former banker, Rurik Jutting, appeared in a Hong Kong court charged with murdering two Indonesian women found in his Wan Chai apartment. Police discovered one body on the floor and another in a suitcase on the balcony after Jutting called them to the scene. The hearing was adjourned until May pending the analysis of forensic evidence.

A massive tornado killed one person and destroyed homes in Illinois, cutting a 22-mile path through Ogle County. The storm flattened a local restaurant and left responders searching for trapped residents, though officials credit early warnings with saving lives. Severe weather also touched down across several other Midwestern states.

Don McLean's original manuscript for "American Pie" sold for $1.2 million at a Christie's auction. The 16-page draft achieved the third-highest auction price for an American literary manuscript. McLean, 69, said he sold the document to provide for his family.

The user wants a 2-3 sentence news wire style summary of this article. Key facts:
- UNRWA Commissioner-General Pierre Krähenbühl making emergency visit to Yarmouk Palestinian refugee camp in Syria on Saturday
- 18,000 civilians remain, including 3,500 children
- Camp controlled mostly by ISIS and Al-Nusra Front (90%)
- Population dropped from 160,000 to 18,000
- Cut off from aid since November 2013, reports of malnutrition

Terse news wire style. Let me draft:

"The head of the U.N. relief agency for Palestinian refugees will make an emergency visit Saturday to Syria's Yarmouk camp, where 18,000 civilians, including 3,500 children, remain amid fighting. ISIS and Al-Nusra Front militants control some 90% of the camp, which has been largely cut off from aid since November 2013. The camp's population has fallen from 160,000 to about 18,000 since the Syrian conflict began in 2011."

That's three sentences, terse, wireThe head of the U.N. Palestinian refugee agency will make an emergency visit Saturday to Syria's Yarmouk camp, where 18,000 civilians, including 3,500 children, remain amid the conflict. ISIS and Al-Nusra Front militants control about 90% of the camp, which has been largely cut off from aid since November 2013. The camp's population has fallen from 160,000 to roughly 18,000 since fighting began in 2011.

Saudi-led airstrikes targeting Houthi positions in Sanaa have killed hundreds and cut power to millions. The International Committee of the Red Cross warns of a humanitarian crisis as aid deliveries remain stalled. Deposed President Hadi remains in exile as ground fighting intensifies across the country.

Legendary former Australia cricket captain and broadcaster Richie Benaud has died aged 84 after battling skin cancer. Benaud, who never lost a Test series as captain, became the sport's most iconic commentator and was widely mourned by figures including Prime Minister Tony Abbott.

A total lunar eclipse, the shortest of the century, is visible across western North America and parts of South America and Asia. The nearly five-minute celestial event is the third in a four-eclipse sequence known as a tetrad.

Real estate heir Robert Durst was indicted by a federal grand jury for unlawful possession of a firearm. The charge follows his arrest in New Orleans, where he awaits extradition to Los Angeles to face a first-degree murder charge.

Paul Walker's final film, "Furious 7," opens Friday, serving as an emotional tribute to the late actor. Producers used script rewrites, special effects, and Walker's brothers as body doubles to complete his scenes and respectfully retire his character. The release prompts widespread mourning and remembrance from fans and co-stars honoring the beloved actor, who died in a 2013 car crash.

"The Price Is Right" model Manuela Arbelaez accidentally revealed a game's correct answer, inadvertently awarding a contestant a new car. Host Drew Carey laughed off the on-air blunder, and Arbelaez later tweeted that everything turned out fine.

Thai Smile Airways unveiled an Airbus A320 featuring "Adventure Time" livery and interior branding. The Cartoon Network-themed plane is part of a partnership with the new Cartoon Network Amazone water park in Pattaya. The inaugural flight from Bangkok to Phuket is scheduled for April 4.

Pedestrians in Washington, D.C., stopped traffic to help a mother duck and her ducklings safely cross a busy street. CNN journalists witnessed bystanders using an umbrella to corral the birds and escort them to a nearby grassy area.

French police have concluded evidence collection at the Germanwings crash site, leaving private security to guard the remaining debris. Investigators have recovered both black boxes and isolated 150 DNA profiles from the 150 victims killed when co-pilot Andreas Lubitz deliberately downed the plane.

Cuba attended the Summit of the Americas for the first time since 1962 as the U.S. moves toward restoring diplomatic ties. The White House is expected to remove Cuba from the state sponsor of terrorism list, a key Cuban demand for reopening embassies. Tensions remain, however, as Cuba continues to back ally Venezuela despite ongoing U.S. disputes with Caracas.

Jesus’ itinerant ministry relied on a common purse funded by wealthy patrons and female supporters like Mary Magdalene and Joanna. Despite preaching the perils of wealth, the movement required substantial donations to maintain its subsistence-level operations.

California regulators ordered Pacific Gas & Electric Co. to pay a record $1.6 billion penalty for unsafe gas pipeline operations linked to a 2010 San Bruno explosion that killed eight people. The majority of the penalty will fund mandated pipeline safety infrastructure improvements.

Lauren Hill, the 19-year-old college basketball player who realized her dream of playing despite a terminal brain cancer diagnosis, has died. Hill inspired millions by playing in a specially scheduled NCAA game and helped raise $1.4 million for pediatric cancer research.

A massive fire broke out Friday morning at the General Electric Appliance Park in Louisville, Kentucky. Firefighters responded to the four-alarm blaze, though no injuries were reported. The cause of the fire remains under investigation.

Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif received a hero's welcome following the recent nuclear framework agreement. Lesser-known facts about Zarif include his U.S. education, a past tweet acknowledging the Holocaust, and an early role in revolutionary student takeovers of Iranian consulates. He continues to work closely with U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry ahead of a June 30 deadline.

A Connecticut judge denied a motion to release 17-year-old "Cassandra C." from state custody, where she remains forced to undergo chemotherapy for Hodgkin lymphoma. The teen is in remission and scheduled to complete treatment next month, though her attorneys criticized the ruling and called the hospital "effectively jail."

New psychological computer analysis confirms the 1728 play "Double Falsehood" was primarily written by William Shakespeare and John Fletcher. Researchers found the linguistic signatures of both playwrights dominate the work, largely exonerating publisher Lewis Theobald of forgery claims. The findings add a new work to Shakespeare's literary canon.

French and German media reports claim a cell phone video showing the final moments of the Germanwings crash exists, but French prosecutors and investigators deny any such footage has been recovered or analyzed. Lufthansa confirmed that co-pilot Andreas Lubitz had previously suffered from severe depression, though the airline stated he was fit to fly.

American Samoans are suing the federal government in the D.C. Circuit to secure U.S. citizenship rights under the Fourteenth Amendment. The lawsuit challenges a century-old legal precedent rooted in racial discrimination that currently denies them voting rights. A ruling in the case, which would make American Samoa the last U.S. territory to receive automatic citizenship, is expected imminently.

Blue Bell Creameries has shut down its Broken Arrow, Oklahoma, plant following the discovery of listeria contamination linked to products served at a Kansas hospital. The CDC warned consumers to avoid specific 3-ounce servings from the facility, though the investigation into the exact source of illnesses linked to three deaths remains ongoing. The company has initiated a recall for the affected products, marking the first such action in its 108-year history.

The user wants a 2-3 sentence news wire style summary of this article about the Al-Shabaab attack on Garissa University College in Kenya.

Key facts:
- Al-Shabaab claimed attack on Garissa University College in eastern Kenya
- Many killed, hostages taken
- Somalia-based group, linked to al-Qaeda, has history of attacks in Kenya including Westgate 2013
- Attack targeted Christians, part of broader regional instability

News wire style is terse, factual, front-loads key info. Let me draft:

"Somalia-based Al-Shabaab has claimed responsibility for an attack on Garissa University College in eastern Kenya that left many dead and others held hostage. The al-Qaeda-linked group, which has carried out a string of attacks in Kenya including the 2013 Westgate mall massacre, reportedly separated Christian from Muslim students during the assault. Analysts say the attack reflects deepening regional instability and warn that lasting security requires addressing underlying political and economic exclusion."

That's 3 sentences, terse, wireSomalia-based Al-Shabaab has claimed responsibility for an attack on Garissa University College in eastern Kenya that left many dead and others taken hostage. The al-Qaeda-linked group, which has staged a string of attacks in Kenya including the 2013 Westgate mall massacre, reportedly separated Christian from Muslim students during the assault. Analysts say the attack underscores worsening regional instability and warn that lasting security requires addressing the political and economic exclusion that fuels the group's recruitment.

The U.S. will protest to Moscow after a Russian fighter jet intercepted an American reconnaissance plane over the Baltic Sea in international airspace Tuesday. The Pentagon deemed the maneuver "unsafe and unprofessional," while Russia claims the U.S. aircraft had its transponder off.

A hooded black angel artwork appeared near where Walter Scott was fatally shot by police in North Charleston. Creator Phillip Hyman crafted the reclaimed wood piece to mourn Scott's death, and it has since been adopted as an icon by Black Lives Matter protesters.

A bystander's video contradicted police reports in the fatal shooting of an unarmed black man by a white North Charleston officer. Officer Michael Slager was fired and charged with murder after the footage showed him shooting Walter Scott in the back as he fled. The witness who recorded the video said Scott never grabbed the officer's Taser, directly contradicting Slager's initial statement.

ISIS claimed it seized parts of Iraq's largest oil refinery in Baiji, releasing images purportedly showing the assault. Iraqi security officials denied the claim, insisting government forces remain in full control of the strategic facility.

Nashville's district attorney banned prosecutors from offering female sterilization in plea deals, sparking public outrage over a practice experts say is likely constitutional and historically applied to men. The debate highlights a potential gender bias, as the sterilization of male criminals has long been accepted without similar controversy. The author argues that waiving Eighth Amendment rights via plea bargains makes such punishments legally permissible.

The West African Ebola outbreak has infected over 25,000 people and killed more than 10,000 in the past year. Weekly infections have dropped to 30, the lowest figure since last May, with Liberia and Sierra Leone decommissioning surplus treatment facilities. However, unsafe burials and unidentified transmission chains in Guinea continue to pose a threat of new infections.

The NCAA claims it has no legal duty to ensure the academic integrity of student-athletes, despite its public commitment to education. This assertion comes in response to a lawsuit regarding the University of North Carolina academic fraud scandal. Critics argue the organization is contradicting its core principles to avoid liability.

An explosion at a controversial chemical plant in southeastern China injured six people and sparked a major fire, which is now under control. The blast occurred at a paraxylene facility in Zhangzhou city following an oil leak. The plant was previously relocated due to public protests over pollution concerns.

A defense attorney argues that mandatory police body cameras could prevent tragedies like the Walter Scott shooting and restore public trust. The author contends that while the devices are costly, they are necessary to curb racial bias and reduce the use of excessive force by law enforcement. The op-ed emphasizes that video evidence serves as a crucial interim solution to deep-seated systemic issues.

The VII Summit of the Americas in Panama is overshadowed by rising tensions between the U.S., Cuba, and Venezuela. While a historic handshake between President Obama and Cuban President Raul Castro was expected to dominate, Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro's accusations of U.S. interference and Cuba's public support for Venezuela have created a diplomatic "triangle of tension."

A fire broke out on a nuclear submarine undergoing repairs at a Russian shipyard, reportedly due to welding work on rubber insulation. Officials stated there was no ammunition or nuclear fuel on board and that the incident caused no injuries or environmental threat.

Weakened Tropical Storm Maysak, formerly a super typhoon, approached the Philippines Saturday, prompting flood and landslide warnings. Authorities barred outdoor activities and ordered precautionary evacuations ahead of its expected landfall Sunday morning. Officials warned residents to prepare for potential heavy impact despite the storm's loss of intensity.

NFL legend Deion Sanders publicly chastised his son on Twitter for claiming to eat "hood doughnuts," reminding him of his wealthy upbringing. Sanders tweeted that his son is a "Huxtable with a million $ trust fund" and should "stop the hood stuff."

Guatemala faces epidemic levels of gender-based violence rooted in a post-war culture of impunity and machismo, with two women killed daily. Despite government reforms and grassroots efforts to support survivors, systemic weaknesses leave 98% of cases unresolved. Victims like Adelma Cifuentes are breaking the silence, but advocates warn that international attention is urgently needed.

Police in Malegaon, India, are requiring residents to register their cattle in a photo database to enforce a state-wide beef ban. The mandate follows a recent slaughter case and the passage of strict laws criminalizing the killing and consumption of cows, bulls, and bullocks. Beef traders have ended a month-long strike in protest and vowed to challenge the ban in court.

Police in Lucknow, India, have acquired pepper-spraying drones to control violent mobs and unruly protests. The new crowd-control measure has drawn criticism from civil liberties advocates who question the aggressive tactic and lack of regulation.
Don McLean's handwritten lyrics for "American Pie" sold for $1.2 million at Christie's. The 16-page manuscript for the 1971 cultural anthem was purchased by an unnamed buyer.

A sophisticated gang executed a daring Easter weekend heist in London's jewelry district, stealing from safety deposit boxes in a manner reminiscent of the 1971 Baker Street robbery. Former Scotland Yard commander Roy Ramm suggests such meticulously planned crimes typically rely on inside information and close-knit teams rather than opportunistic criminals. Police are now conducting an intense forensic investigation, focusing on potential inside involvement to identify the perpetrators.

7-Eleven is hosting its first "Bring Your Own Cup" Slurpee Day on Saturday from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. For $1.49, customers at participating U.S. stores can fill their own containers, provided they are sanitary and fit through a 10-inch in-store display hole. The promotion kicks off peak Slurpee season and is separate from the traditional Free Slurpee Day held in July.

Former Kentucky State Senator Georgia Davis Powers criticizes Rand Paul's presidential campaign launch, arguing his record contradicts his message of inclusion. She cites his past questioning of the Civil Rights Act and voting rights protections as evidence he would take the country backward. Powers concludes that Paul's policies are disqualifying and that voters deserve better.

A passenger was killed and the driver injured when a Lamborghini crashed at Walt Disney World Speedway on Sunday. The fatal accident occurred during the Exotic Driving Experience, a program allowing customers to drive exotic sports cars on a racetrack.

The defense rested Monday in the murder trial of former NFL star Aaron Hernandez, who is accused of killing Odin Lloyd. Jurors will soon deliberate the largely circumstantial case, weighing key evidence including disputed home security footage and a footprint matching Hernandez's shoes. Hernandez also faces separate double murder charges pending the outcome of this trial.

Chinese authorities have detained five feminist activists for "creating disturbances" ahead of International Women's Day, with their fate expected by April 13. The detentions coincide ironically with Beijing's anticipated passage of an anti-domestic violence law and the 20th anniversary of a major UN women's conference hosted in China. The crackdown reflects a broader government effort to strangle independent activism.

Former Maryland Governor Martin O'Malley challenged the "inevitability" of Hillary Clinton's presidential candidacy during a trip to Iowa. He argued that history shows frontrunners are not unbeatable and called for a robust primary contest. O'Malley's comments come as Clinton prepares to launch her campaign despite his low polling numbers.

Former NFL player Aaron Hernandez was sentenced to life in prison for the 2013 murder of Odin Lloyd. Lloyd's family delivered emotional testimony in court, remembering him as a devoted family man and gifted athlete. Lloyd's mother expressed forgiveness for those involved in her son's killing.

Senator Ted Cruz courts evangelical voters in Iowa, adopting a pastoral style to energize the state's influential Christian base. Facing a crowded GOP field, Cruz aims to win the caucuses by uniting social conservatives with the tea party and libertarian factions. His strategy relies on mobilizing millions of evangelical voters who have historically stayed home on Election Day.

- 978 migrants rescued Friday in Mediterranean, 30 miles off Libya coast, per Italian Coast Guard
- Italy registered 10,000+ arrivals in Q1 2015; 2,000 rescued first weekend of April

News wire style is terse, factual, lead with the most important info. Let me draft:

"Italian Coast Guard rescued 978 migrants in the Mediterranean on Friday, picking them up 30 miles off the Libyan coast. Italy has registered more than 10,000 migrant arrivals in the first three months of 2015, with most coming from West Africa, Somalia and Syria via Libya. At least 480 migrants have died making the crossing this year, up from fewer than 50 at the same point in 2014, the International Organization for Migration said."

That's three sentences, terse, wireItalian Coast Guard rescued 978 migrants in the Mediterranean on Friday, picking them up 30 miles off the coast of Libya. Italy registered more than 10,000 migrant arrivals in the first three months of 2015, with most coming from West Africa, Somalia and Syria via Libya. At least 480 migrants have died crossing the Mediterranean this year, up from fewer than 50 at the same point last year, the International Organization for Migration said.

French television network TV5Monde gradually restored operations Thursday after a cyberattack knocked 11 channels off the air. ISIS logos appeared on the network's social media accounts, though no group immediately claimed responsibility. The "extremely powerful" attack disrupted broadcasts reaching 260 million homes worldwide.

Director David Lynch has exited Showtime's upcoming "Twin Peaks" revival, citing insufficient funding. The network expressed sadness over the departure but stated it still hopes to resolve the dispute. Lynch confirmed the third season may continue without him.

High-profile trials for Boston Marathon suspect Dzhokhar Tsarnaev and former NFL player Aaron Hernandez move to jury deliberations in Massachusetts. Sen. Rand Paul officially launched his presidential campaign, while Chicago voters cast ballots in a mayoral runoff. Ferguson residents head to the polls in a local election heavily influenced by the Michael Brown shooting protests.

Severe storms spawned multiple tornadoes across Kansas and Missouri overnight, causing wind damage, flooding, and large hail. Forecasters warn that dangerous nighttime tornadoes and additional severe weather will continue threatening the Midwest and surrounding river valleys through Thursday.

Jodi Arias was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole for the 2008 murder of her ex-boyfriend. A judge handed down the maximum sentence after two previous juries deadlocked on the death penalty. Arias will serve her sentence at the Arizona State Prison Complex-Perryville.

A Delaware family fell seriously ill after being exposed to methyl bromide, a restricted toxic pesticide, at a U.S. Virgin Islands luxury villa. The EPA is investigating whether an improper indoor fumigation by Terminix caused the exposure, while the Justice Department has launched a criminal probe.

A Columbia Journalism School review concluded that Rolling Stone's retracted article on an alleged UVA gang rape was a failure of reporting and editing. The Phi Kappa Psi fraternity is considering legal action, though defamation laws present hurdles regarding the sueability of groups and governmental entities. While the university cannot sue, individual fraternity members may have a case if they can prove specific damages.

FBI agents shot and captured a suspect linked to 32 armed robberies following a confrontation in Georgia. Two agents were injured when the suspect rammed their vehicles while attempting to flee. The injured agents were released from the hospital, and the suspect's wounds are not life-threatening.

An Alaska Airlines flight returned to Seattle shortly after takeoff Monday after the pilot heard banging from the cargo hold. A ramp agent who had fallen asleep while loading luggage was found in the pressurized compartment and later discharged from a hospital. The airline is investigating the incident.
